units.text: . Introduction A One-Dimensional Lake Model in ECCC's Land Surface Prediction System

In Canada, almost 9% of the land surface area is covered by inland lakes (Atlas du Canada: https://www. rncan.gc.ca/cartes-outils-et-publications/cartes/latlas-canada/10802) with high lake density in Boreal regions (Verpoorter et al., 2014). The sheer quantity of lakes in Canada makes them a central part of the Earth System in this part of the world. In Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) at Environmental and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), efforts have been mainly dedicated at land and ocean surfaces with less focus on lakes until recently. In most ECCC's current operational systems, inland water physical processes are simulated using a simple water scheme. Evaporation from water bodies is calculated based on water surface temperatures and ice cover fractions that are initialized daily using analyses (Brasnett & Surcel Colan, 2016;Buehner et al., 2016) once a day. These analyses use observations where available, mainly over large and/or easily accessible lakes. A climatology is used for observation-free lakes, which constitute a very large proportion of all lakes. The Canadian Ice Service (CIS), for example, monitors approximately 300 lakes out of close to 900,000 lakes in Canada. The majority of the simulated lakes in Canada are thus non-responsive to short-term variations in weather forcings because the lake-atmosphere exchanges are driven by lake surface conditions that come from a climatology.

Improved computer power and model resolution now enable lakes to be appropriately accounted for. NWP centers around the world have started implementing one-dimensional lake models in their forecasting systems over the past decade (Brown & Duguay, 2010;Dutra et al., 2010;LeMoigne et al., 2016;Mallard et al., 2014;Rooney & Jones, 2010) with a positive impact on forecast errors, especially during spring and summer (Balsamo et al., 2012). ECCC also recognizes the need for interactive lakes in its NWP systems as well as its environmental prediction systems, such as those used to forecast surface conditions and floods. ECCC'S Water Cycle Prediction System (WCPS; Durnford et al., 2018) already uses NEMO for the Great Lakes (Madec et al., 2008) but the smaller lakes are still simulated using the simple water scheme mentioned earlier. The Canadian Small Lake Model (CSLM;MacKay, 2012;MacKay et al., 2017), an interactive one-dimensional dynamic lake model, was thus recently implemented in ECCC's Surface Prediction System (SPS; Leroyer et al., 2011;Bernier et al., 2014) as a first step toward the goal of replacing the non-interactive water scheme for all lakes that cannot be simulated with NEMO due to its computational cost. The current study aims at evaluating the impact of replacing the simple water scheme -and the ice and lake water temperature analyses it uses -by CSLM in an offline context (i.e., uncoupled to the atmosphere) on lake surface conditions: water temperature, ice phenology, near-surface atmospheric conditions. The article is organized as follows: the surface modeling platform SPS, the lake model CSLM, experimental setup and evaluation data sets are presented in Section 2, evaluation results related to the lake surface water temperature, the ice cover and the near-surface conditions are analyzed in Section 3, and results are summarized and discussed in Section 4.
Models and Methods
Surface Prediction System

ECCC's Surface Prediction System (SPS; also known as GEM-Surf; Bernier et al., 2014;Garnaud et al., 2017;Leroyer et al., 2011) is used operationally and for research purposes at resolutions ranging from 25 km to 100 m. SPS is a driver used to simulate conditions at, near and under the surface when forced by atmospheric conditions. It consists of four main components: (a) schemes to simulate the temporal evolution of the soil and surface processes, (b) atmospheric forcings (i.e., surface pressure, near-surface air temperature and humidity, wind, solar and longwave radiation, and precipitation), (c) geophysical characteristics, and (d) initial conditions for the surface schemes.

In SPS, the surface heterogeneity is represented at subgrid scales as an aggregation of different covers (i.e., land, urban, water, continental ice, and sea ice). Each type of cover (or tile) features specific input parameters and parameterization schemes to simulate the related physical processes (Essery et al., 2003;Molod & Salmun, 2002;Rochoux et al., 2015). As previously mentioned, inland water physical processes are simulated using a simple water scheme. Evaporation from water bodies is calculated based on water surface temperatures and ice cover fractions that are updated daily using analyses (Brasnett & Surcel Colan, 2016;Buehner et al., 2016).

The ice cover fraction analysis is produced operationally at ECCC at a 10-km resolution globally using a 3D-Var assimilation method with satellite-derived data from the Special Sensor Microwave Imager (SSMI and SSMIS), Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT), the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2) and in situ observations from the Canadian Ice Service (CIS). As detailed in Buehner et al. (2016), the analysis is designed to gradually return to climatology if there are no new observations, which is true over a large proportion of lakes across Canada. The climatology is derived from Interactive Multisensor Snow and Ice Mapping System (IMS) and CIS data over the 2007-2017 period. ECCC also produces a global water surface temperature analysis operationally at a 0.1-degree resolution using an optimal interpolation (OI) technique to assimilate remotely sensed from the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), and AMSR2, as well as in situ data (from buoys, boats, etc.), and a return to climatology when no data are available. This climatology is based on averages of the HadISST1 (Hadley Centre Sea Ice and SST) monthly analyses (Brasnett, 2008) over the 1992-2011 period. It also uses the ice cover analysis described above to refine the final product, as fully described in Brasnett and Surcel Colan (2016). These analyses will be referred to as ICE-SST analyses from this point onwards.
The current study aims at evaluating the impact of replacing the simple water scheme-and the ice and lake water temperature analyses it uses-by a one-dimensional dynamic lake model: the CSLM.
Canadian Small Lake Model

The CSLM is a one-dimensional thermodynamic lake scheme made up of three basic components: a thermal model, a turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) based surface mixed layer model, and a snow and ice model (Figure 1). The complete nonlinear surface energy balance is computed in a thin (5 cm) surface skin layer, and the one-dimensional heat equation is solved in the water column based on the computed surface temperature and penetrating shortwave radiation (MacKay, 2012). Shortwave extinction follows Beer's Law with up to 3 bands allowed. However, following MacKay (2012) and MacKay et al. (2017) the solar flux is partitioned (roughly equally) into two bands with extinction coefficients of 0.9 m −1 and 6.9 m −1 fixed throughout the domain. The equation of state follows Farmer and Carmack (1981) but neglects pressure effects and salinity. A diurnal surface mixed layer is computed based on the integrated TKE approach of Imberger (1985) and Spigel et al. (1986)-complete details of which can be found in MacKay (2012). In addition to the forced convective mixing provided by the TKE model, free convection (gravitational instability) takes place whenever dense water overlies lighter water.

The thermal model is solved on a uniform grid with a user specified number of layers and mesh size, the latter of which is normally taken to be 0.5 m in order to reasonably resolve diurnal surface layer mixing and deepening processes. This immediately leads to computational cost issues for very deep lakes which would require a large number of layers at such a high resolution to reach lake bottom. As CSLM is primarily intended as a component in a numerical weather or climate prediction system which must be computationally efficient, a compromise must be decided: in the present study a maximum depth of 10 m (i.e., 20 layers) is used. Note that in a similar study with CSLM over western Canada little difference was found when maximum lake depths were increased from 10 to 50 m . The development of a stretched grid to handle more efficiently the inclusion of deep lakes while maintaining high resolution near the surface is currently an active area of research. The boundary condition at lake bottom is generally taken to be adiabatic, but the option to include a sediment heat flux is now available (MacKay, 2019). This option is not employed in the current study.

Because ice and snow play such an important role in the thermodynamics of many lakes, a comprehensive snow and ice physics module is included in CSLM (MacKay et al., 2017). It consists of the complete snowpack physics component of the Canadian Land Surface Scheme (CLASS; , a white-ice (i.e., snow-ice) production scheme, as well as a conventional congelation ice production scheme. Snow is modeled as a separate thermal layer from ice, and the model allows for both fractional ice cover as well as fractional snow-on-ice cover. The lake surface may thus contain open water, bare ice, and snow covered ice simultaneously under appropriate circumstances, with each surface type associated with distinct turbulent heat and moisture flux exchange with the atmosphere.

One-dimensional thermodynamic lake models generally do not attempt to parameterize ice mechanics and thus do not represent fractional ice cover: lakes are normally considered completely ice free or completely ice covered (e.g., Mironov et al., 2010;Subin et al., 2012). This has serious consequences for simulations of large lakes, where ice-on dates have been found to be biased early, sometimes by as much as 2 months (Pietikainen et al., 2018). Other studies have had to artificially reduce lake ice and snow albedos in order to represent the impact of partially open water (e.g., LeMoigne et al., 2016). In CSLM, a simple fractional ice cover scheme based on a scaling argument presented in Lepparanta and Wang (2008) is employed. In this approach, ice is assumed to raft or ridge (and thus produce open water leads) until it grows to a critical thickness, H crit , based on the fetch L of the lake:

where τ a is the scale of the surface wind stress (taken to be approximately 0.15 Pa), and P* is the compressive strength of ice, currently set to 27.5 kPa (e.g., Hibler & Walsh, 1982). When the simulated ice thickness H is less than H crit the ice is considered mechanically unstable: it breaks under the action of wind stress and forms pressure ridges (or rafts for very thin ice) and open water leads. Experimental Setup
For the current study, SPS is run twice over a domain covering most of Canada and Northern USA with a horizontal resolution of 2.5 km from 1 September 2015 to 31 August 2018.
Geophysical Fields

Both SPS simulations use the same geophysical fields. Topography information is obtained from the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) GTOPO30, which is a global digital elevation model with a horizontal grid spacing of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 km). The soil composition comes from the Global Soil Data for Earth system modeling (GSDE; Shangguan et al., 2014) with a horizontal grid spacing of 30 arc seconds. It relies on the most accurate soil texture data at the time of its creation. The vertical variation of soil property is captured by eight layers to the depth of 2.3 m. Surface cover type is given by the 300-m resolution European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (CCI_LC, v1.6.1). For the purpose of this study, the CCI_LC data set has been enhanced by replacing its lake cover information by the HydroLAKES data set (Messager et al., 2016). HydroLAKES is a database providing information on all global lakes with a surface area of at least 10 ha, including estimates of average lake depth. As detailed in Messager et al. (2016), the average depth of large lakes (with a surface area ≥500 km 2 ) is obtained from the literature, while for smaller lakes, the average depth was estimated using a geostatistical model based on surrounding land surface topography. In this study, HydroLAKES database has further been enhanced by replacing average depths values of large lakes by using the 3 arc-second (approx. 90 m) resolution bathymetry data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI; https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/mgg/greatlakes/greatlakes.html).

To better understand and evaluate the impact of lake modeling, the lakes are divided into different categories depending on their surface area and depth, as detailed in Table 1. Figure 2 depicts lake properties over the study domain in terms of lake depth and surface area. Over 64% of all lakes over the study domain are subgrid lakes (less than 6.25 km 2 ) and close to 64% of all lakes are shallow lakes (less than 5 m deep). 52% of all lakes are both subgrid and shallow lakes.

As explained in Section 2.2, the temperature profile of lakes is only simulated up to a depth of 10 m in this study's configuration of CSLM. Therefore, in addition to Figure 2, Table 2 provides the percentage of lake-covered grid points corresponding to different depth categories up to 10 m within each category of surface area (subgrid, intermediate and large). For example, 59% of all grid points covered by subgrid lakes have a lake depth between 2.5 and 5 m, and more than 89% of large lake grid points have a lake depth of 10 m or more. . Average depth (in meters) of (b) subgrid (surface area less than 6.25 km 2 ), (c) intermediate (between 6.25 and 6,000 km 2 ), and (d) large (greater than 6,000 km 2 ) lakes.
Atmospheric Forcings

ECCC's High Resolution Deterministic Prediction System (HRDPS v4; Milbrandt et al., 2016;Faucher, 2016), the 2.5-km version of the Global Environmental Multiscale (GEM) model (Mailhot et al., 2006), is used to drive the evolution of the land surface state simulated by SPS in external mode. Downwelling shortwave and longwave radiation and surface pressure are taken at the surface, while air temperature, specific humidity, and wind are taken from GEM's lowest vertical level, which is roughly at 20 m for temperature and humidity and 40 m for wind, all from HRDPS lead times 06-12 hr. As detailed in Bernier et al. (2014), the downscaling procedures of forcing data are embedded within SPS, including interpolation to the high-resolution surface of air temperature, surface pressure, and specific humidity. With respect to precipitation, the forcing data come from the Canadian Precipitation Analysis (CaPA; Mahfouf et al., 2007;Fortin et al., 2015). CaPA combines a short-range 6-hr HRDPS precipitation forecast with available precipitation gauge observations using an optimum interpolation (OI) methodology. The precipitation analysis does not provide phase information; SPS uses the surface air temperature and a 0-degree Celsius threshold to differentiate rain from snow. To avoid interpolation of forcings to drive SPS, the study domain in this study is exactly colocated with the HRDPS domain.
Initial Conditions

All SPS simulations in this study are initialized in the same manner, except for lake variables. Surface and sub-surface variables (ground temperature, snow depth, soil water content, etc.) are initialized using a previously run analysis valid for the start date of the simulations (i.e., 1 September 2015). When CSLM is not used to simulate the evolution of lake variables, lake surface temperature and lake ice fraction are initialized using the ICE-SST analyses (see Section 2.1). When CSLM is used, the lake water temperature profile is initialized to 277 K and the surface water temperature (LSWT) to 275 K. The ice fraction is set to zero and the TKE to 1 × 10 −12 J/kg. For all simulations, the first year (i.e., 1 September 2015-31 August 2016) is used as a spinup for the system to reach equilibrium. The evaluation of the impact of the 1-D lake model is thus performed over the following 2 years (1 September 2016-31 August 2018).
Experiments

Two experiments have been run for this study, using SPS v5.9.9 with the CSLM module. The reference simulation (CSLM_off) is with SPS in its standard configuration, which includes the use of the simple water scheme and the ICE-SST analyses to initialize it. CSLM is not called to simulate inland water in this simulation. The other SPS experiment makes use of CSLM to simulate the evolution of lake variables (CSLM_on) with a variable lake depth as defined by the Hydrolakes and NCEI data described in Section 2.3.1. To summarize, both simulations use SPS with the same geophysical fields, the same atmospheric forcings, and surface variables are initialized in the same manner, except for lake variables. Note that CSLM_off is reinitialized daily based on data assimilation, through the use of the ICE-SST analysis, but CSLM_on is run open loop for the entire period and is never reinitialized.
Evaluation Data Sets

CSLM has been evaluated at specific lakes in past studies (MacKay, 2012;MacKay et al., 2017). However, the goal of the current study is to evaluate the model across most of Canada and Northern USA for its future use in the Canadian Meteorological Center's operations at ECCC. Large-scale data sets are therefore necessary, and these generally involve satellite-based data.

Two challenges arise from this necessity. First, current satellites are configured to supply data with a resolution that is not fine enough to detect subgrid lakes, which constitute nearly two thirds of the lake grid points  of the domain. This causes an evaluation that is unavoidably biased toward larger lakes. Second, the ICE-SST analysis, used to initialize and update lake variables in CSLM_off, includes data from numerous satellites (see Section 2.3.1), thus strongly limiting the possibilities for an independent evaluation. It will inherently be biased toward CSLM_off, which benefits from observations on larger lakes. Nonetheless, the evaluation against satellite-based observations will complement lake-specific studies toward a pan-Canadian view of the impact of the 1-D lake model on lake behavior (surface temperature, ice cover) and surrounding near-surface conditions (2-m temperature and humidity).

Lake surface water temperature (LSWT) observations are obtained from the Sentinel3/SLSTR sensor (https://land.copernicus.eu/global/products/lswt). It is a global 1-km data set available in near-real time since November 2016. The sea surface temperature (SST) from NOAA's ACSPO VIIRS data set is also used to evaluate the model outputs. It is a global data set with a resolution that ranges from 0.75 to 1.5 km depending on the position within the swath. These data are the same as the one used to produce the ICE-SST analysis (see Section 2.1). To facilitate the comparison with the simulated data, the Sentinel3 and ACSPO VIIRS data are upscaled to the 2.5-km simulation grid using a mode (or majority) resampling method where the value that appears most often of all the sampled points is selected. Figure 3 shows the evolution in time of the number of grid points containing observed lakes in the VIIRS and Sentinel3 data sets with a indication of the distribution of lake surface area. In winter, this number decreases due to ice cover, which prevents satellites from measuring surface water temperature. Subgrid lakes (shown in turquoise) are mostly unobserved by the two satellites. Sentinel3 data, not included in the ICE-SST analysis, covers more lakes across the study domain that VIIRS data, which will allow an evaluation at grid points not covered by VIIRS.

The ice cover fraction observational data to evaluate the model simulations is from the IMS Daily Northern Hemisphere Snow and Ice Analysis (https:// nsidc.org/data/g02156). It covers the northern hemisphere from 1997 to present day, although the 1-km product (used in the current study) is only available since December 2014. IMS data are produced by analysts who evaluate a variety of real-and near-real time fields, including satellites, models and station reports, and data sources change over time. This data set is also upscaled to the model grid using a mode resampling method. Figure 4 shows  the distribution of IMS-observed grid points that include lakes. Close to 70% of all IMS-observed lakes have a depth equal to or greater than 10 m, and only 5% of all IMS-observed lakes are subgrid lakes.

Near-surface observations are obtained from multiple networks: the Surface Weather OBservations (SWOB), MEteorological Terminal Aviation Routine weather reports (METAR), and the surface SYNOPtic observations (SYNOP). These in situ observations are gathered and archived operationally at ECCC, and allow for a point-bypoint evaluation of 2-m temperature (TT) and humidity (TD) where data are available. Since these observing sites generally need human intervention, they are relatively fewer in number in Northern Canada.
Results

The evaluation presented in this section is to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of CSLM across the pan-Canadian domain and to assess its future potential in ECCC's earth system models. Lake water surface temperature, lake ice cover, 2-m temperature and 2-m humidity are all variables that strongly impact interactions between the land surface and the atmosphere. The full lines refer to the comparison of simulated data against all available Sentinel3 data, while dashed lines refer to the comparison of simulated data against Sentinel3 data only when not colocated with VIIRS data. The dashed lines allow for a more independent evaluation since VIIRS data are included in the ice cover analysis used to initialize CSLM_off, and one can make the assumption that colocated VIIRS and Sentinel3 data will provide a similar LSWT signal. Subgrid lakes are not shown since too few are observed by either satellites.
Lake Surface Water Temperature

Along with Figures 5 and 6, Table 3 gives the average values of LSWT bias, STDE, RMSE (all in K) during the ice-free season of both 2017 and 2018, for large and intermediate lakes, and for CSLM_off and CSLM_on at grid points where Sentinel3 data are available but VIIRS data are not (i.e., dashed lines on Figures 5 and 6).

On large lakes, CSLM_off presents a negative bias of about 2-3 K. The use of CSLM increases the lake surface water temperature, enough to produce a positive bias that is larger in value than in CSLM_off: 4-5 K. The positive bias is greatest during the early months of the ice-free season (until mid-July approximately). The STDE is however improved through the use of CSLM. Overall, it is reduced by about 0.9 K in 2017 and 0.4 K in 2018, and Figure 5 shows that the reduction in STDE in CSLM_on starts as early as June. The combined effect of the degraded bias and improved STDE leads to a slight degradation of the RMSE in the early months of the ice-free season, and a neutral to positive impact on the RMSE from mid-July onwards.

On intermediate lakes, the use of CSLM produces a clear improvement in terms of LSWT bias, STDE and RMSE during the ice-free season. The warming of LSWT in CSLM corrects the strong negative bias in CSLM_off from −5.5 to 1.2 K in 2017 and from −5.0 to 1.4 K in 2018. The STDE in CSLM_on starts the ice-free season with greatest values than CSLM_off (see Figure 6, but becomes lower than CSLM_off around early June during both years). CSLM is able to reduce the STDE by 1.3 and 1.5 K in 2017 and 2018, respectively, with maximum values reaching 2 K. In terms of RMSE, CSLM_on is constantly better than CSLM_off, except for a few days in early May 2018, with an overall 46% reduction in 2017 and a 38% reduction in 2018.
Ice Cover

Lake ice cover is a key variable controlling lake-atmosphere exchanges of heat and humidity. Both simulations are thus evaluated against observation-based IMS data from September 2016 to August 2018. Since IMS data are a binary product using 40% fractional cover as a threshold, the same threshold is used to evaluate simulated data using a contingency table (see Table 4). Figure 7 shows the proportion of lake grid points that fall within one of the four contingency table categories: hit, miss, false alarm and correct negative. The lakes are separated into lake area categories: subgrid, intermediate and large lakes. For subgrid lakes, which represent only 5.3% of IMS-observed lakes as shown in Figure 4, the use of CSLM greatly increases the hits over the two winters of the study period, from 28.2% in CSLM_off to 46.9% in CSLM_on, while reducing the proportion of correct negatives by about 10%. Even though there is an overall decrease in false alarm values, the strong decrease of about 19% in misses is in part counterbalanced by a 10% increase in false alarms in CSLM_on. As shown in In large lakes, the use of CSLM has an overall negative impact. Although it reduces false alarms and increases correct negatives, it increases misses and reduces hits. This is reflected in degraded ice cover ETS and FBI on large lakes, as shown in Table 5. It is important to note however that in large lakes, CSLM is "competing" against the numerous observations in the ICE-SST analysis used to initialize CSLM_off once per day. Furthermore, the nature of this evaluation does not reflect the dynamic nature of ice, particularly on large lakes. CSLM, being a 1D lake model, calculates ice cover at each grid point based on the total surface of the lake (which may cover multiple grid points). IMS data, on the other hand, make use of observed data that reflect ice accumulation and drifts caused by currents and winds. To take this into account, another type of evaluation is performed over the nine large lakes of the study domain. Over each of these lakes, simulated data are treated as IMS data where a fractional ice cover less than 40% is translated into 0 and an ice cover greater or equal to 40% into 1. The values of all grid points that cover the lake are then averaged to obtain a single ice fraction per day per lake. A similar operation was performed on IMS data: an average ice fraction is calculated each day using each grid point covered by a specific lake. CSLM_on however is not able to portray ice fraction as well, particularly when Lake Erie froze over in 2018. In more remote lakes (Winnipeg, Athabasca, Great Slave and Great Bear), in situ observations are scarce and the ICE-SST analysis relies more heavily on satellite observations of these lakes as well as observations of surrounding water bodies (i.e., the Arctic Ocean and Hudson Bay), which may explain why CSLM_off never reaches a full ice cover as shown by observations. In these lakes, CSLM_on is able to better represent the evolution of ice fraction, particularly on lakes Athabasca and Great Slave.

The timing of ice-on is generally slightly too early in CSLM_on, particularly in northernmost lakes, with a mean bias of about 10 days. With respect to ice-off, CSLM also tends to melt the ice slightly too early in northernmost lakes, while melting is on point in southernmost lakes except in Lake Ontario in 2018.
Near-Surface Atmospheric Conditions

Both lake surface water temperature and ice cover have a direct impact on the exchanges of heat and humidity with the atmosphere. Since SPS is an offline system (i.e., there is no feedback from the surface to the atmosphere), in which no information is passed laterally amongst grid points, the simulated heat and humidity fluxes are a result of atmospheric forcings as well as surface conditions and variables. The presence of a lake will thus only impact grid points with a lake fraction, meaning that the only way to evaluate the effect of CSLM on near-surface conditions is through observing sites that are located within grid points with a lake fraction. Note. IMS data's 40% threshold to define whether a grid point is ice free or ice covered is also used for simulated data.  A similar evaluation has been performed on the simulated 2-m dew-point temperature (TD). In this case, CSLM has very little impact, except in summer near subgrid lakes where it tends to reduce the warm bias present in CSLM_off by about 0.2 K (data not shown). Since TD is an indirect measure of humidity fluxes between the surface and the atmosphere, the total evapotranspiration per season averaged over grid points containing lakes is shown in Figure 10. The warmer lake surface temperatures (Figures 5 and 6) during the summer months are well reflected in the increased humidity fluxes (up to 38%) in CSLM_on compared to CSLM_off. In winter, the greater ice coverage in CSLM_on, seen in Figures 7 and 8, results in an near-interruption of the net evapotranspiration: 3 mm in winter 2017 and 1 mm in winter 2018.
Discussion and Conclusions

In most of ECCC's current operational systems, inland water physical processes are simulated using a simple water scheme. Water surface temperatures and ice cover fractions are updated daily using analyses. However, ECCC recognizes the need for interactive lakes in its NWP systems as well as its environmental prediction systems, such as those used to forecast surface conditions and floods. The CSLM, a one-dimensional dynamic lake model, was thus recently implemented in ECCC's SPS as a first step toward this goal. The current study evaluates the impact of replacing the simple water scheme -and the ice and lake water temperature analyses it uses -by CSLM on a large scale and in an offline context (i.e., uncoupled to the atmosphere) on lake surface conditions: water temperature, ice phenology, near-surface atmospheric conditions.

With respect to lake surface temperature, the use of CSLM introduces a warm bias during ice-free months and significantly reduces the STDE, which results in a decreased RMSE from July to September approximately. The positive lake water surface temperature bias in CSLM_on has a direct impact on the 2-m air temperature by reducing the cold bias observed in CSLM_off. The use of CSLM tends to reduce the bias and STDE of near-surface temperatures during the summer months, with improvements that increase with the size of nearby lakes. The comparison with IMS ice cover data showed that CSLM improves ice cover in subgrid lakes, while having a neutral impact on intermediate lakes. On large lakes, CSLM tends to degrade ice cover simulation in southernmost lakes, where many observations are available and integrated in CSLM_off, while improving ice cover in northernmost lakes such as Great Slave and Athabasca lakes. The timing of ice-on is generally slightly too early in CSLM_on, particularly in northernmost lakes, which confirms the findings from MacKay et al. (2017). Some of the error in ice phenology is undoubtedly due to the simplified ice mechanics adopted here, a subject that will be reported on in a forthcoming manuscript. Overall, CSLM increases lake ice cover, particularly over subgrid lakes and in the northern latitudes, which has a strong impact on humidity fluxes between the surface and the atmosphere during the wintertime with a near-interruption of evapotranspiration over lakes. In summertime, the increased lake surface water temperature leads to a 38% increase in evapotranspiration in CSLM_on.

Due to the nature of observations used in this study, the evaluation is inherently biased toward the larger lakes of the domain, which are less numerous (see Figure 2) but more difficult to simulate with a 1D lake model, because of the predominance of 3-dimensional exchanges in larger lakes. Martynov et al. (2012) pointed out that since 1-D lake models do not take 3-D mixing processes into account, they are not able to simulate the thermodynamic balance and feedbacks between the lakes and the atmosphere appropriately. The use of a 3-D lake model for the very large lakes is thus recommended, and what is currently done in ECCC'S Water Cycle Prediction System (WCPS; Durnford et al., 2018), which uses NEMO for the Great Lakes (Madec et al., 2008).

Nonetheless, CSLM has shown its potential in simulating lake surface conditions over most lakes and in particular over subgrid lakes, which constitute the largest proportion of lakes in Canada. In order to benefit from CSLM's strengths, the next step is its implementation in the Canadian Land Data Assimilation System (CaLDAS; Carrera et al., 2015;Carrera et al., 2019). It will allow for lake-related data assimilation when and where observations are available: mostly in populated areas for in situ observations and on relatively large lakes for satellite-derived data. As an example, observed data could facilitate the correction of bias in ice phenology. It is expected that the synergy of the interactive dynamic lake model CSLM and lake-related observations, as well as the use of NEMO for the larger lakes, will improve the simulation and initialization of lake conditions in ECCC's systems.

Future studies will also include a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of dynamic lakes on the atmosphere within ECCC's 3D Earth system model GEM, such as the High Resolution Deterministic Prediction System (HRDPS; Milbrandt et al., 2016). Studies such as Bischoff-Gauß et al. (2006) and Balsamo et al. (2012) have shown that lakes not only have an impact on near-surface conditions and the boundary layer, but also up to the troposphere (Balsamo, 2013) and on large scale precipitation (Martynov et al., 2012). The introduction of interactive lakes in an Earth System also entails an impact on the hydrological cycle, including the net basin supply and streamflow. Work is currently underway at ECCC to find an efficient way to couple lakes to the river network, and thus improve environmental predictions across Canada.

As a result of the uni-directional coupling of the surface and the atmosphere within the framework of SPS, CSLM shows very little impact on near-surface temperature when the evaluation is performed at all observing sites (top row) as expected. The improvement in bias brought by CSLM is particularly noticeable in sites close to intermediate and large lakes, where the time average bias is reduced from −0.74 to −0.68 K in CSLM_off, respectively, to 0.03 K in both case in CSLM_on. This warming of near-surface conditions in CSLM_on is in direct agreement with the warm bias in LSWT observed inFigures 5 and 6, which is based on an evaluation comprised mostly of data on large and intermediate lakes. The standard deviation of the error is slightly reduced in intermediate and large lakes when using CSLM, particularly during the months of March to July, with a time-average improvement of 0.21 K near intermediate lakes and 0.29 K near large lakes.
